binding_the_audit_carried: Verify each row against the thing it claims closed it, not against its own CLOSED marker. A row that merely says CLOSED is not proof. Deleting a live debt row is worse than leaving a closed one: if a row turns out to be live, refuse it and report.

reusable_failure_mode: TWO OF FIVE were mis-scored by the audit, both the same way: a debt row's CLOSED marker covered SUB-PARTS while the row's TITLE named the part still open. In both, the row's own body said so a few hundred characters later -- 'but (3) stays open', '-- open: the durable fix' -- but a scan that stops at the bold CLOSED reads the row as settled. Neither row would have survived a line-number-and-marker sweep. The rule this produced: a struck-through title and the word CLOSED are not evidence; read the row to its end, then check the artifact it names against the thing it claims closed it. Note that both refusals were also the rows whose titles state a defect in the PRESENT tense -- a title that still describes something true is the cheapest available signal that a row is live.
scope_discipline: The audit deliberately scoped the sweep to rows it had verified. Twenty-two struck-through rows remain in the table, unverified and untouched by design, logged as their own debt row for a later pass. Given that two of five proposals here scored wrong, widening the sweep on the implementer's own initiative would have been the expensive mistake.
